description: Bitter grey-green leaves off the meadow scrub. Good in stew, better in a poultice, and a handful will put you down.
lore: The women who sell it count the leaves into your hand out loud. That is not ceremony. Three in a pot of stew is a good dinner. A dozen crushed into a wet rag is the best thing going for a bad shoulder. A fistful, chewed, and you go down — properly down, on your face, in the road — and come back together beside the nearest fire some hours later, [[lore/the_quiet|the way anyone does]], pockets intact, a hole where your evening was, and a little less of whatever you had been thinking about.

One man worked that out and made a habit of it. Pleasant, paid without haggling, back every few weeks and lighter each time. The trade argued about him for a winter and came out with a rule it keeps still: they will sell you your fistful. They will not sell you the second, they will not say who might, and every woman on that road knows his face.
gm_notes: What a poison can do in a country where nothing dies: cost you an evening and a little of what you were carrying in your head. The rule is care, not punishment. He is still out there and still pleasant.
